chunks.text: An antiderivative reverses differentiation: F(x) is an antiderivative of f(x) if F'(x) = f(x).
Antiderivatives are never unique, because adding any constant does not change the derivative.
Every function has a whole family of antiderivatives of the form F(x) + C, differing only by a constant.
The constant of integration +C must be included on every indefinite integral, and represents real content such as an unknown initial value.
Graphically, the family of antiderivatives is infinitely many copies of the same curve shifted vertically, all with identical slopes at each x.
An initial condition like F(0) = 50 selects one specific antiderivative by determining the value of C.
The indefinite integral is written ∫f(x) dx, where f(x) is the integrand and dx indicates the variable of integration.
The reverse power rule: ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, valid for all n except n = −1.
The exception ∫x⁻¹ dx = ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C, since the power rule would divide by zero when n = −1.
The absolute value in ln|x| keeps the antiderivative of 1/x valid for negative x.
∫cos x dx = sin x + C, because the derivative of sin x is cos x.
∫sin x dx = −cos x + C, because the derivative of −cos x is sin x; forgetting the negative sign is a common error.
∫sec²x dx = tan x + C, because the derivative of tan x is sec²x.
∫eˣ dx = eˣ + C, since eˣ is its own derivative.
The constant multiple rule lets you pull constants outside: ∫k·f(x) dx = k·∫f(x) dx.
The sum and difference rule lets you integrate term by term: ∫[f ± g] dx = ∫f dx ± ∫g dx.
When integrating a sum, write only one +C at the end, since the sum of several arbitrary constants is one arbitrary constant.
Example: ∫(3x² − 5 sin x + 7) dx = x³ + 5 cos x + 7x + C, where the −5 times −cos x becomes +5 cos x.
There is no product rule or quotient rule for antiderivatives; products and compositions require techniques like u-substitution.
Any antiderivative can be verified by differentiating it to recover the original integrand.
Every continuous function has an antiderivative, guaranteed by the accumulation function F(x) = ∫ from a to x of f(t) dt, whose derivative is f(x).
Some antiderivatives exist but cannot be written in closed form, such as the antiderivative of e^(−x²), which is why numerical integration is needed in practice.
